The Italian Renaissance, spanning the fourteenth to sixteenth centuries, was a cultural and artistic movement originating in Italy that marked the rebirth of classical learning and values and fundamentally transformed European art, literature, and philosophy. Centered in Florence, Venice, and Rome, it produced innovations in perspective, anatomy, and the human figure that broke decisively with medieval tradition and established the foundations of modern Western art. The movement's embrace of individual genius, scientific observation, and the dignity of human life defined the modern world.

The Italian Renaissance emerged in Florence in the fourteenth century as scholars and artists rediscovered classical Greek and Roman texts, philosophy, and aesthetic principles after centuries of medieval tradition. Linear perspective was formalized by Filippo Brunelleschi and theorized by Leon Battista Alberti, allowing artists to represent three-dimensional space on a two-dimensional surface with mathematical precision.

The Renaissance pioneered oil painting as a dominant medium, adapted from Flemish techniques, which allowed for unprecedented luminosity, layering, and subtlety impossible with tempera. It celebrated anatomical accuracy achieved through direct observation of the human body, including dissection, allowing artists to render figures with unprecedented naturalism and dignity.

The High Renaissance, circa 1495 to 1520, was the period's culmination, when Leonardo, Michelangelo, and Raphael created their greatest works in Florence, Rome, and Milan. The Renaissance was centered on Florence and patronage by the Medici family, whose wealth and taste shaped the movement and allowed artists to work with unprecedented resources and freedom.

The Italian Renaissance revived classical motifs from ancient Greece and Rome, mythology, philosophy, and proportions, integrating them with Christian subject matter in a synthesis unique to the Renaissance. It established the concept of the artist as intellectual and genius, not merely a craftsman, a radical elevation that gave artists social status and authority over their work's meaning. The movement extended beyond Italy across the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries to transform art throughout Europe, making Florence and Rome the center of artistic innovation.
